meta.topic: Two-week BA sprint for a Payment API integration

problem:
Northgate Retail needs a Payment API integration delivered in a two-week sprint. The retailer's checkout must submit payment instructions to Crestline Bank, receive a clear acceptance or rejection, and create the order only when the payment outcome is known. The sprint has a fixed end date because the retailer has a trading peak approaching, and the team is small: one business analyst, two developers, one tester and a part-time architect. The product owner has a long list of wants, the bank's API documentation is mostly complete but silent on several edge cases, and nobody has yet agreed what the API response actually promises: receipt, validation, acceptance or completion.

The learner must run the sprint as a business analyst, not as a bystander. That means discovery and analysis in the first days, documentation that developers can build from, design and refinement with the bank's integration team, development support during the build, and SIT, UAT and release readiness before the sprint ends. The case tests prioritisation under a fixed deadline: the sprint cannot deliver everything, so the analyst must separate the minimum viable integration from the nice-to-have features, and must surface the risky unknowns early, such as what happens when the API returns success but the order is not created, and what happens when SIT passes but production behaves differently.
solution:
Start the sprint with discovery compressed into the first two days: confirm the business outcome, the checkout journey, the payment types in scope, the expected volumes, and the response contract. The contract question matters most: agree in writing what each response means, so that an acceptance response is never mistaken for completion, and define the status enquiry path the retailer uses when a response is missing. Clarify the edge cases with the bank early: timeouts, duplicate submissions, callbacks that never arrive, and amounts near the product limits. Write the analysis as buildable documentation: field definitions, validation rules, error codes, idempotency, correlation IDs, and acceptance criteria in Given When Then form.

During development, support the developers daily: answer questions the same day, refine stories as the bank's answers arrive, and keep the documentation current when a decision changes. Plan SIT around the integration boundaries, not only the happy path: test each failure mode, each error code and each retry. Run UAT with real checkout journeys and production-shaped data, and check release readiness before the sprint ends: environment parity, certificates, credentials, rate limits, monitoring, rollback and the support runbook. If scope must be cut, cut features, never the failure handling, the reconciliation or the release evidence, and record the cut with the product owner.

decision.question: Northgate Retail needs a Payment API integration with Crestline Bank delivered in a two-week sprint before a trading peak. The checkout must submit payments, receive a clear outcome, and create orders only when the payment outcome is known. You are the business analyst on a small team with a fixed end date.

options.label: A
options.detail: Accept the full product owner list into the sprint and work longer hours to deliver it all.

options.label: B
options.detail: Build the happy path only and handle failures after go-live, since the peak is approaching.

options.label: C
options.detail: Write the full specification first and start development only when it is complete, since accuracy matters more than the sprint date.

options.label: D
options.detail: Prioritise the minimum viable integration, clarify the response contract and edge cases early, support development daily, and gate release on SIT, UAT and readiness evidence.

decisionRationale: Option D is correct because a fixed-date sprint needs ruthless prioritisation, early clarification of the risky unknowns, and a release gate based on evidence. Option A overloads the sprint and guarantees a late or broken delivery. Option C spends the sprint writing and leaves no time to build or test. Option B ships a checkout that cannot handle the failures customers will actually meet.

steps.title: Confirm business outcome, journey, scope and response contract in sprint days one and two
Clarify edge cases with the bank integration team and document decisions
Write field definitions, validation, errors, idempotency and acceptance criteria
Build the integration with daily analyst support and refinement
Run SIT across happy path, failure modes, retries and callbacks
Run UAT with real checkout journeys and confirm release readiness
Accept or cut scope on evidence and approve the release decision

happy: The sprint delivers a working integration that submits payments, interprets responses correctly, handles timeouts, duplicates and missing callbacks, and creates orders only when the payment outcome is known. SIT and UAT evidence is filed, the release checklist passes, and the deferred scope is recorded with the product owner rather than silently dropped.

negative.title: API returns success but no order is created
negative.detail: The response promises receipt, but the event or callback that creates the order is lost. Trace the correlation ID across gateway, service, event bus and order system, reconcile the financial effect, and recover the order exactly once.

negative.title: SIT passes but production fails
negative.detail: Production differs in configuration, certificates, network or data. Compare environments before blaming code, and retest with production-shaped payloads.

negative.title: Pre-production data mismatch near go-live
negative.detail: SIT and UAT passed but pre-production data does not match. Assess whether the mismatch is representative and release-critical, and delay or proceed only through formal risk acceptance.

negative.title: Scope pressure threatens failure handling
negative.detail: The product owner asks to cut error handling to fit more features. Refuse the cut: failure handling, reconciliation and release evidence are part of the minimum viable integration.

technical: Keep one contract record with the API version, the field definitions, the validation rules, the error catalogue, the idempotency rule, the correlation ID flow and the status enquiry path, all versioned together. Persist the idempotency key, payload hash, correlation ID, original payment reference and outcome for every submission, and log the request and response at each boundary. Store SIT and UAT evidence with build version, environment and date, and keep the release checklist with the parity, certificate, credential and monitoring checks signed off.

accounting: A payment accepted by the API but not yet confirmed must not create an order, and an order must not be created twice from a retried submission. The retailer and the bank reconcile on the correlation ID and the payment reference, and ambiguous payments sit in a controlled recovery state with a service level for resolution. Operations need a worklist of unreconciled submissions, monitoring on callback and event delivery, and a runbook that tells support exactly what to check before telling a customer the payment succeeded or failed. The sprint's success is measured by clean reconciliation after the peak, not only by a launch on the planned date.

scenarios.when: the retailer acts on the response,
scenarios.then: it treats the response as receipt or acceptance as the contract states, and confirms completion through status enquiry or events.

scenarios.when: the order system checks the payment,
scenarios.then: it uses the correlation ID and status enquiry to determine the outcome before creating or cancelling the order.

scenarios.given: a pre-production data mismatch is found,
scenarios.then: unexplained material differences block approval until resolved or formally risk-accepted.

questions.question: What must be agreed first about an API response?
options: What the response promises: receipt, validation, acceptance or completion
The colour of the checkout button
questions.explanation: The response contract defines what success means, and mistaking receipt for completion is how orders are created for payments that never completed.

questions.question: What should be cut first when a fixed-date sprint is overloaded?
options: Features outside the minimum viable integration
questions.explanation: Features can be deferred, but failure handling, reconciliation and release evidence are part of the minimum viable integration.

questions.question: Why is SIT alone not enough evidence for go-live?
options: Production can differ in configuration, certificates, network, limits and data
SIT never tests the happy path
questions.explanation: SIT passing does not prove production will behave the same way, because environments differ in ways that only parity checks and pre-production testing expose.

questions.question: How should a missing callback be handled?
options: Trace the correlation ID and use status enquiry to determine the outcome
questions.explanation: A missing callback leaves the outcome unknown, so the correlation ID and status enquiry must establish it before the order is created or the payment is retried.
